overview: Malta is a small island country in the Mediterranean Sea, south of Sicily. Its capital, Valletta, is one of the smallest capital cities in Europe. Malta was ruled for centuries by the Knights of St John and later by Britain, and it became independent in 1964. Maltese and English are its official languages. Malta joined the European Union in 2004.

geography.text: Malta is an archipelago with three inhabited islands: Malta, Gozo and Comino. The islands are low and rocky, with no rivers or lakes, so much of their fresh water comes from taking the salt out of seawater. The coast has cliffs, bays and deep natural harbours, including Valletta's Grand Harbour.

subsections.title: Climate
subsections.text: Hot, dry summers and mild winters; it hardly ever freezes.

subsections.title: Wildlife
subsections.text: Malta is a stopping point for migrating birds, and its seas are home to dolphins and turtles.

history.text: Malta's prehistoric temples are among the oldest free-standing buildings in the world. The islands were ruled by Phoenicians, Romans, Arabs and Normans, and in 1530 were given to the Knights of St John, who held off a huge Ottoman siege in 1565. Britain took Malta in 1800, and it became independent in 1964 and a republic in 1974.

events.title: Temple builders
events.text: The first of Malta's great stone temples, such as Ġgantija, are built around this time.

events.title: Knights of St John
events.text: The knights are given Malta as their new home.

events.title: The Great Siege
events.text: The knights and the Maltese defeat a huge Ottoman invasion.

events.title: The George Cross
events.text: Britain awards the whole island a medal for bravery during wartime bombing.

government.text: Malta is a parliamentary republic. Its House of Representatives chooses the Prime Minister, and the President, elected by parliament, is head of state. Malta became a republic in 1974, joined the European Union in 2004 and uses the euro. It is the smallest country in the EU.

economy.text: Tourism, financial services and online gaming companies are the biggest parts of Malta's economy. Its position in the middle of the Mediterranean makes it important for shipping, and Malta has one of the largest ship registers in the world.

culture.text: Maltese is the only official language of the European Union that comes from Arabic, and it is written in the Latin alphabet. Malta's prehistoric temples are older than Stonehenge and the Egyptian pyramids. Valletta, the capital, was built by the Knights of St John after 1565.

items.title: Megalithic temples
items.text: Built from about 3600 BC, among the oldest free-standing buildings in the world.

items.title: Valletta
items.text: A fortified city built by the Knights of St John.

items.title: The Maltese language
items.text: A Semitic language with many Italian and English words.

subsections.title: Food
subsections.text: Pastizzi, pastries filled with ricotta or peas, and rabbit stew, the national dish.

subsections.title: Music and arts
subsections.text: Baroque churches, filled with art by painters such as Caravaggio, are found across the islands.

subsections.title: Traditions and festivals
subsections.text: Each village holds a festa for its patron saint, with marching bands, fireworks and decorated streets.

sport.text: Football is the most popular sport in Malta, which has followed English and Italian football passionately for decades. Water polo is popular in summer.

items.title: Water polo
items.text: A summer sport played by clubs from harbour towns.

didYouKnow: Malta's temples are older than Stonehenge and the pyramids of Giza.
Malta has no rivers or lakes; much of its water comes from turning seawater into fresh water.
